value.overview: The Eastern Meadowlark is a medium-sized grassland bird in the blackbird family, Icteridae, despite its lark-like name. It is recognized by its richly streaked brown back, bright yellow throat and breast, and bold black V-shaped chest marking. Its clear, plaintive song is often delivered from a fence post or other exposed perch. The species occupies open country across much of the Americas and includes resident tropical populations as well as migratory northern populations.
value.classification: Eastern Meadowlark, Sturnella magna, belongs to the order Passeriformes and the family Icteridae. It is closely related to the Western Meadowlark but is a distinct species.
value.identification: Adults have heavily streaked brown upperparts, a pointed bill, a brown-and-white head pattern, and bright yellow underparts marked by a prominent black V across the breast. A pale or white stripe borders the yellow throat, helping separate it from the Western Meadowlark. White outer tail feathers are conspicuous in flight. Males and females look alike, although females are usually slightly smaller and may appear less strongly marked. Juveniles are duller and more heavily brown overall.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from eastern and central North America south through Mexico and Central America, with additional populations in the Caribbean and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, recorded especially in open lowland and foothill country, including pastures, agricultural fields, wet grasslands, savannas, and other grassy areas. It avoids dense forest and generally needs broad fields with enough vegetation for cover and ground foraging. Costa Rican populations are associated with the Central Pacific and other suitable open regions and may be locally distributed.
value.migrationStatus: Northern populations are short-distance or partial migrants, moving south in autumn and north in spring. The population occurring in Costa Rica is considered resident rather than a regular seasonal migrant, although local movements may occur in response to weather, food, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Eastern Meadowlarks nest on the ground in grasslands and pastures. The female selects a shallow depression, sometimes an animal hoofprint, and builds a concealed cup from grasses and plant stems. Some nests have woven roofs or tunnel-like entrances. A clutch usually contains two to seven eggs, which hatch after about 13 to 16 days of incubation. Young leave the nest after roughly 10 to 12 days. Northern birds commonly produce one or two broods; breeding details for Costa Rican populations are less thoroughly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other invertebrates, including grasshoppers, crickets, beetles, caterpillars, grubs, ants, and spiders. The bird also takes seeds, grains, and berries, especially outside the breeding season. It usually feeds by walking slowly through grass, probing soil with its pointed bill, and opening the bill underground to expose prey. In Costa Rica it forages in pastures, field margins, short grass, and seasonally wet open habitats.
value.behavior: Eastern Meadowlarks are primarily ground foragers and often remain inconspicuous among grass until disturbed. Males sing from fence posts, shrubs, utility lines, or other elevated perches and use their songs to defend territories. During courtship and territorial disputes, males may display their yellow breasts and perform short jump flights. Outside the breeding season, birds can gather loosely in suitable fields. When flushed, they fly with rapid, shallow wingbeats followed by short glides.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining overall. North American monitoring has documented a steep reduction in abundance since the late twentieth century, although trends may vary among regions and resident tropical populations are less well monitored.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of grassland habitat are major concerns. Conversion of pastures and native grasslands to intensive agriculture or development, reforestation of abandoned fields, early mowing, heavy grazing, pesticide use, and the loss of dense nesting cover can reduce breeding success. In Costa Rica, continued conversion or intensification of open agricultural and pasture habitats may affect localized resident populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native grasslands, pastures, savannas, and seasonally wet open areas. Maintain some tall, dense vegetation for nesting and avoid mowing or heavily grazing fields during the breeding season where meadowlarks are present. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use, preserve grassy field margins, and support bird monitoring in Costa Rica to clarify local distribution and population trends.
